title: The Commission and the Crossing
subtitle: Joshua 1 to 4
description: God commissions Moses' assistant, two spies find faith inside Jericho, and the Jordan stops at flood stage for a nation's crossing.
paragraphs: The book opens with a death in its first line and a promotion in its second breath. "Now after the death of His servant Moses, the LORD spoke to Joshua son of Nun, Moses' assistant". Forty years of story had filed past this man at Moses' elbow, at the mountain, against Amalek, up the slopes of the spies' mission and down under its sentence, and now the voice that had spoken to Moses spoke to him. Its first sentence was a fact and a starting gun together: "Moses My servant is dead. Now therefore arise, you and all these people, and cross over the Jordan into the land that I am giving to the children of Israel."

The promise came with the old borders attached: "I have given you every place where the sole of your foot will tread, just as I promised to Moses." The territory would run from the wilderness and Lebanon to the great River Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites, and west as far as the Great Sea. And over the borders God laid the promise He had made to Moses at another river and a mountain: "No one shall stand against you all the days of your life. As I was with Moses, so will I be with you; I will never leave you nor forsake you."

Then came the charge Joshua would hear three times in one speech, the sentence this book is built around. "Be strong and courageous, for you shall give these people the inheritance of the land that I swore to their fathers I would give them." Again, with the law attached: "Above all, be strong and very courageous. Be careful to observe all the law that My servant Moses commanded you. Do not turn from it to the right or to the left, so that you may prosper wherever you go." And then the discipline that would carry the courage: "This Book of the Law must not depart from your mouth; meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do everything written in it. For then you will prosper and succeed in all you do." The third time, God made it a question too plain to dodge: "Have I not commanded you to be strong and courageous? Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go."

Joshua's first orders were logistics, not battle. He sent the officers through the camp with a message for every tent: "Prepare your provisions, for within three days you will cross the Jordan to go in and take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess." Three days. After forty years, the deadline was three days.

Then Joshua turned to the tribes already settled, the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh, whose families and herds were staying east of the river in the land Moses had given them. Their bargain from the plains of Moab still stood, and Joshua read it back to them in Moses' own words: "The LORD your God will give you rest, and He will give you this land." Their wives, children, and livestock could remain. But every mighty man of valor was to cross armed ahead of his brothers and fight beside them until the LORD gave the western tribes rest too; only then could the eastern men return to their own inheritance.

Their answer is worth hearing in full, because it is the first time in forty years of story that the people, unprompted and undivided, hand a leader his orders back as obedience. "Everything you have commanded us we will do, and everywhere you send us we will go. Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you. And may the LORD your God be with you, as He was with Moses." And they closed by throwing God's own charge back at the man who had just received it, a blessing shaped like an order: "Above all, be strong and courageous!"

Before the three days ran out, Joshua sent two men secretly from Shittim to inspect the land, especially Jericho. They entered the house of a prostitute named Rahab and stayed there, and the city knew by nightfall. The king of Jericho sent word to her door: "Bring out the men who came to you and entered your house, for they have come to spy out the whole land."

Rahab had already hidden the two men under stalks of flax laid out on her roof. What she told the king's messengers was a lie, and the text reports it without praise and without rebuke: the men had come, she said, she had not known where they were from, and at dusk, as the gate was closing, they had gone out; pursue them quickly and you may catch them. The king's men took the bait and rode for the fords of the Jordan, and the gate of Jericho shut behind them.

Then Rahab climbed to the roof, and the woman inside the enemy's wall made the fullest confession of faith anyone in the book has made yet. "I know that the LORD has given you this land and that the fear of you has fallen on us, so that all who dwell in the land are melting in fear of you. For we have heard how the LORD dried up the waters of the Red Sea before you when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to Sihon and Og, the two kings of the Amorites across the Jordan, whom you devoted to destruction. When we heard this, our hearts melted and everyone's courage failed because of you, for the LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below."

Hear what she had done: from inside Jericho, with nothing but forty-year-old news and recent word from across the river, she had arrived at the sentence Moses spent Deuteronomy teaching Israel to take to heart, that the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth below. And she built a bargain on it. She had shown the spies kindness; now let them swear by the LORD to show kindness to her father's house, a sure sign, her parents and brothers and sisters and all who belonged to them delivered from death.

"Our lives for your lives!" the men agreed, on conditions, and the conditions were as plain as hers. She was to tie a scarlet cord in the window she would lower them through, gather her whole family inside her house, and keep the mission secret. Anyone who went out the door would carry his own blood on his head; anyone harmed inside the house, theirs on the spies'. Then she let them down by a rope through the window, for her house was built into the city wall, and sent them to the hill country to hide three days while the pursuit searched the road and returned empty.

The report the two men brought Joshua was eleven words of news and one of theology, and it inverted the report their fathers' generation had died for. "The LORD has surely delivered the entire land into our hands". And then the sentence underneath the news: "Indeed, all who dwell in the land are melting in fear of us." Forty years before, ten spies had come home saying the people's hearts melted at the giants in the land. These two came home saying the melting was on the other side of the wall.

Early the next morning Joshua left Shittim with all Israel and camped at the Jordan. After three days the officers went through the camp again, and this time the orders were about a piece of furniture: "When you see the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God being carried by the Levitical priests, you are to set out from your positions and follow it. But keep a distance of about two thousand cubits between yourselves and the ark. Do not go near it, so that you can see the way to go, since you have never traveled this way before."

The distance was the point. The ark would go first, half a mile of empty ground behind it, so that the whole nation could watch where the road into the land actually began. Joshua told the people: "Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you." And to Joshua himself, God said the quiet thing underneath the ceremony: "Today I will begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel, so they may know that I am with you just as I was with Moses."

Joshua announced the sign before it happened, the way his master had taught the people to listen. "This is how you will know that the living God is among you and that He will surely drive out before you the Canaanites, Hittites, Hivites, Perizzites, Girgashites, Amorites, and Jebusites. Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth will go ahead of you into the Jordan." Twelve men were chosen, one from each tribe, for work not yet explained. Joshua said that the moment the priests' feet touched the water, "its flowing waters will be cut off and will stand up in a heap."

The timing was the worst of the year, and the text makes sure we know it: "Now the Jordan overflows its banks throughout the harvest season." Not a low summer ford but a river in flood. The priests reached the edge, and "as soon as the priests carrying the ark reached the Jordan and their feet touched the water's edge," the flow stopped. The water coming down "stood still. It backed up as far upstream as Adam, a city in the area of Zarethan, while the water flowing toward the Sea of the Arabah (the Salt Sea) was completely cut off. So the people crossed over opposite Jericho."

The priests did not hurry across. "The priests carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firm on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan, while all Israel crossed over the dry ground, until the entire nation had crossed the Jordan." A nation walked through a stopped river in sight of Jericho's walls, and the men holding the ark stood in the middle of it until the last Israelite was through.

Before the priests came up, there was work for the twelve men. Each was to carry a stone from the middle of the Jordan, from the very place the priests stood, one stone per tribe on a man's shoulder, and set them down where the nation would spend the night. Joshua gave them the reason in advance, and it was a reason aimed at children not yet born: the stones were "to serve as a sign among you. In the future, when your children ask," and here the future question stands in the text: "What do these stones mean to you?" The answer was prescribed just as carefully: "The waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD. When it crossed the Jordan, the waters were cut off." And then the verdict on the pile: "Therefore these stones will be a memorial to the Israelites forever."

Joshua did something more, and it was not in the orders. "Joshua also set up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan, in the place where the priests who carried the ark of the covenant stood. And the stones are there to this day." Two memorials for one crossing: one at the camp, where children would ask about it, and one in the riverbed, where the returning water would cover it the moment the priests stepped out. The second pile was for no audience the text names.

The eastern tribes crossed too, armed before Israel as Moses had instructed, about forty thousand troops ready for battle crossing "before the LORD into the plains of Jericho." Then the priests were called up, and the day's two promises closed at once: "When the priests carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD came up out of the Jordan and their feet touched the dry land, the waters of the Jordan returned to their course and overflowed all the banks as before." And the narrator records the other fulfillment in the same breath as the first: "On that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel, and they revered him all the days of his life, just as they had revered Moses."

It was the tenth day of the first month, the very date on which, a generation earlier, Israel had chosen its Passover lambs in Egypt. The nation camped at Gilgal, on the eastern border of Jericho, and there Joshua set up the twelve stones. His teaching about them reached further than the camp that heard it: when children ask their fathers, "What is the meaning of these stones?" the answer is to begin with a dry riverbed: "Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground." And then the comparison the answer itself builds in: "For the LORD your God dried up the waters of the Jordan before you until you had crossed over, just as He did to the Red Sea, which He dried up before us until we had crossed over." And the purpose of the pile outlasted the crossing itself: "He did this so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, and so that you may always fear the LORD your God."

Behind Israel, the Jordan ran at flood again, closed like a door. In front of Israel, a few miles west, stood Jericho, its gate shut since the spies came. Between the river and the wall lay the camp at Gilgal, and the first Passover in the land was four days away.

title: Gilgal, Jericho, and the Sin in the Camp
subtitle: Joshua 5 to 8
description: A circumcised camp, the last manna, a silent march around Jericho, one man's hidden theft, and the law read between two mountains.
paragraphs: The first news out of Gilgal belonged to the enemy. "Now when all the Amorite kings west of the Jordan and all the Canaanite kings along the coast heard how the LORD had dried up the waters of the Jordan before the Israelites until they had crossed over, their hearts melted and their spirits failed for fear of the Israelites." What Rahab had reported from one rooftop was true of a whole coastline. Israel had crossed without striking a blow, and the land was already afraid.

What Israel did next was not attack. "At that time the LORD said to Joshua, "Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel once again."" The reason takes the story back forty years: every man circumcised in Egypt had died in the wilderness, and the sons born on the journey had never been circumcised along the way. So at a hill the text names Gibeath-haaraloth, Joshua circumcised the new generation with knives of stone, and the whole nation stayed in camp, inside enemy country, until they were healed. God's comment on the rite reached back past the wilderness to the slavery itself: "Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you." The place took its name from the sentence: Gilgal. It was a strange first act for an invasion. Before Israel had won a single battle, its army lay wounded in an open camp within reach of Jericho's walls, marked with the covenant sign before it was armed with a victory.

Four days after the crossing date, on the evening of the fourteenth day of the month, Israel kept the Passover at Gilgal on the plains of Jericho, the first in the land. The next day they ate the land's own produce, unleavened bread and roasted grain. And then, quietly, a forty-year era ended at breakfast: "And the day after they had eaten from the produce of the land, the manna ceased. There was no more manna for the Israelites, so that year they began to eat the crops of the land of Canaan." No announcement, no ceremony. The bread from heaven stopped because the bread of Canaan had started.

Before Jericho, Joshua met someone. Near the city he looked up and saw a man standing in front of him with a drawn sword, and Joshua, who did not yet know who he was facing, asked the soldier's question: "Are You for us or for our enemies?" The answer refused the terms of the question: "Neither," He replied. "I have now come as Commander of the LORD's army." Joshua fell facedown and asked what his Lord had to say to His servant, and the Commander gave him the sentence Moses had heard at a burning bush: "Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy." And Joshua did so. The assistant had become the man standing on holy ground, and the army he led had just been reclassified: it belonged to a Commander above him.

"Now Jericho was tightly shut up because of the Israelites. No one went out and no one came in." God's plan for the shut city sounded like no siege ever fought: march around it once a day for six days, seven priests with seven rams' horns before the ark, and on the seventh day circle it seven times, then a long horn blast and a mighty shout from everyone at once: "Then the wall of the city will collapse and all your people will charge straight into the city."

Joshua added one order of his own, and it may have been the hardest to keep: "Do not give a battle cry or let your voice be heard; do not let one word come out of your mouth until the day I tell you to shout. Then you are to shout!" So for six days an army marched around a walled city in silence, horns sounding, saying nothing, and went back to camp. On the seventh day they rose at dawn and circled seven times, and after the seventh circuit Joshua gave the word and the terms together: "Shout! For the LORD has given you the city! Now the city and everything in it must be devoted to the LORD for destruction. Only Rahab the prostitute and all those with her in her house will live, because she hid the spies we sent."

And he gave a warning that the rest of this episode hangs on: "But keep away from the things devoted to destruction, lest you yourself be set apart for destruction. If you take any of these, you will set apart the camp of Israel for destruction and bring disaster upon it. For all the silver and gold and all the articles of bronze and iron are holy to the LORD; they must go into His treasury."

The horns blew, the people shouted, and the wall collapsed, and the army charged straight in. What followed is told in one unflinching verse: "With the edge of the sword they devoted to destruction everything in the city", and the text lists man and woman, young and old, oxen, sheep, and donkeys. Nothing is softened and nothing is celebrated; the sentence stands as the record of what devoted to destruction meant in practice.

The spies kept their oath in the middle of it. They brought Rahab out, her parents and brothers and all who belonged to her, and settled the family outside the camp. The city was burned, the metals went into the treasury of the LORD's house, and Joshua pronounced a curse over the ruins: "Cursed before the LORD is the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho; at the cost of his firstborn he will lay its foundations; at the cost of his youngest he will set up its gates." Of Rahab the narrator adds the longest view in the book so far: she "has lived among the Israelites to this day." And of Joshua: "So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame spread throughout the land."

Then the story turns, and it turns in the narrator's first sentence, which tells the reader a secret the army did not know: "The Israelites, however, acted unfaithfully regarding the things devoted to destruction. Achan son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of what was set apart. So the anger of the LORD burned against the Israelites."

No one in the camp knew. Joshua sent spies to the next target, Ai, a small town near Bethel, and they came back with the confidence Jericho had bought: "There is no need to send all the people; two or three thousand men are enough to go up and attack Ai. Since the people of Ai are so few, you need not wear out all our people there." About three thousand went up, and Ai's men routed them and killed about thirty-six, chasing them down the slopes. The narrator reaches for the word that has belonged to Jericho all book long and puts it on Israel: "So the hearts of the people melted and became like water."

Joshua tore his clothes and lay facedown before the ark until evening, the elders with dust on their heads beside him, and his prayer was an accusation wrapped in grief: "O, Lord GOD," he said, "why did You ever bring this people across the Jordan to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites to be destroyed? If only we had been content to stay on the other side of the Jordan!" And at its end, the appeal Moses used to make: "When the Canaanites and all who live in the land hear about this, they will surround us and wipe out our name from the earth. Then what will You do for Your great name?"

God's answer began by standing him up. "Stand up! Why have you fallen on your face? Israel has sinned; they have transgressed My covenant that I commanded them, and they have taken some of what was devoted to destruction. Indeed, they have stolen and lied, and they have put these things with their own possessions." The defeat at Ai had not been a failure of tactics. "I will no longer be with you unless you remove from among you whatever is devoted to destruction."

The removal was a narrowing, done by lot in the morning, tribe by tribe, clan by clan, family by family, man by man. Judah was taken. Then the Zerahites. Then the family of Zabdi. Then one man stood where the narrowing ended: Achan. Joshua's words to him were not a shout but an appeal, and they gave the guilty man the dignity of a confession instead of a denial: "My son, give glory to the LORD, the God of Israel, and make a confession to Him. I urge you to tell me what you have done; do not hide it from me."

Achan did not hide it. "It is true," he said. "I have sinned against the LORD, the God of Israel. This is what I did: When I saw among the spoils a beautiful cloak from Shinar, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels, I coveted them and took them. They are hidden in the ground inside my tent, with the silver underneath." Messengers ran to the tent, and it was all there, exactly as confessed. They spread the goods before the LORD, and Joshua and all Israel took Achan to the Valley of Achor with the silver, the cloak, the gold, his sons and daughters, his animals, his tent, everything he owned. Joshua's sentence named the exchange: "Why have you brought this trouble upon us?" And then: "Today the LORD will bring trouble upon you!" All Israel stoned him, and over him they raised a large pile of rocks, and the narrator's refrain sounds again: the pile "remains to this day", and the valley is called Achor, trouble, "to this day."

Ai still had to be taken, and this time God gave a strategy instead of a ceremony and changed one term of engagement: "Do not be afraid or discouraged. Take the whole army with you, and go up and attack Ai. See, I have delivered into your hand the king of Ai, his people, his city, and his land." This city, unlike Jericho, Israel could plunder: "you may carry off their plunder and livestock for yourselves." The devoted things had never been about greed management; they had been about whose the first city was.

The plan was an ambush, thirty thousand men by night behind the city in the traditional reading of the muster, five thousand more between Bethel and Ai, and Joshua's force pretending to break and run as it had in the real defeat. It worked in every detail: the king of Ai emptied his city in pursuit, and God told Joshua, "Hold out your battle lance toward Ai, for into your hand I will deliver the city." The ambush fired the empty city, the fleeing column turned on its pursuers, and the men of Ai were caught between the two forces. Twelve thousand fell that day. "Joshua did not draw back the hand that held his battle lance until he had devoted to destruction all who lived in Ai." The king was hanged on a tree until evening and taken down at sunset, as Moses' law required for a hanged man, and his body was thrown at the city gate under another great pile of rocks, which "remains to this day."

Then, with the war barely started, Israel stopped to do the thing Moses had commanded from across the river years before. On Mount Ebal Joshua built an altar of uncut stones, "an altar of uncut stones on which no iron tool has been used", and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. He inscribed a copy of the law of Moses on stones in the presence of the people. And the nation split in two halves on the facing slopes, half before Mount Gerizim and half before Mount Ebal around the ark, while Joshua read the whole law aloud, all of it: "Afterward, Joshua read aloud all the words of the law", the text says, "the blessings and the curses", "according to all that is written in the Book of the Law." The last word on the day belongs to the completeness of it: "There was not a word of all that Moses had commanded that Joshua failed to read before the whole assembly of Israel, including the women, the little ones, and the foreigners who lived among them."

Three piles of stones now stood in the land: twelve at Gilgal for a crossing, one in the Valley of Achor for a theft, and one at Ai's gate for a hanged king, and the book would keep stacking them. Two cities had fallen and the covenant had been renewed in the middle of the land. What Israel did not know, camped between the mountains, was that the next move in this war would not be made by Joshua at all. It would be made by frightened men from a city a day's walk away, carrying moldy bread.

title: The Gibeonite Covenant and the Long Day
subtitle: Joshua 9 to 10
description: A treaty won by moldy bread, an oath kept anyway, an all-night march to defend it, and a day longer than any before or since.
paragraphs: When the kings west of the Jordan heard what had happened at Jericho and Ai, they did the expected thing: "they came together to wage war against Joshua and Israel." All of them, that is, except one city. "But the people of Gibeon, having heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and Ai, acted deceptively and set out as envoys," and their deception was staged like theater. Worn-out sacks on the donkeys. Old wineskins, cracked and mended. Patched sandals, threadbare clothes, and a whole supply of bread gone dry and moldy. Every prop said the same sentence: we have traveled very far.

At Gilgal they made their pitch: "We have come from a distant land; please make a treaty with us." Israel's first instinct was the right question: "Perhaps you dwell near us. How can we make a treaty with you?" But the Gibeonites had a script for that too. "We are your servants," they said, and when Joshua pressed them on who they were and where they had come from, they answered with the fame of Israel's God, the reports from Egypt and the two Amorite kings east of the Jordan, Sihon and Og. It was a careful speech, and a reader listening closely notices what it never mentions: Jericho. Ai. Anything recent. The news they recited was old enough to have crossed a desert.

Then came the exhibit. "This bread of ours was warm when we packed it at home on the day we left to come to you. But look, it is now dry and moldy. These wineskins were new when we filled them, but look, they are cracked. And these clothes and sandals are worn out from our very long journey."

Israel examined the evidence, and the narrator stops the story cold for the most consequential sentence in the chapter, fifteen words that explain everything that follows: "Then the men of Israel sampled their provisions but did not seek the counsel of the LORD." They tasted the bread. They did not ask God. Joshua made a treaty of peace to let them live, and the leaders of the congregation swore an oath to them by the LORD.

Three days later the truth arrived: the distant foreigners were neighbors, living at Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim, close enough to walk to. The congregation grumbled against its leaders, and the leaders gave an answer that held the whole episode's weight: "We have sworn an oath to them by the LORD, the God of Israel, and now we cannot touch them. This is how we will treat them: We will let them live, so that no wrath will fall on us because of the oath we swore to them." A treaty obtained by lying still bound the people who had sworn it, because the Name attached to it was not theirs to cheapen. The Gibeonites would live, as woodcutters and water carriers for the congregation.

Joshua summoned them and asked the question plainly: "Why did you deceive us by telling us you live far away from us, when in fact you live among us?" Their answer was as honest as their embassy had been false: "Your servants were told clearly that the LORD your God had commanded His servant Moses to give you all the land and wipe out all its inhabitants before you. So we greatly feared for our lives because of you, and that is why we have done this. Now we are in your hands. Do to us whatever seems good and right to you." Joshua confirmed the sentence and the mercy together: they would serve "perpetually" as "woodcutters and water carriers for the house of my God". And the narrator notes they hold that place "for the congregation of the LORD and for the altar at the place He would choose", as they are "to this day." The liars of Gibeon ended up carrying water for the altar of the God they had feared from a distance. It was not the outcome any treaty in the ancient world would have predicted.

The treaty was immediately tested. Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, heard that Gibeon had made peace with Israel, and he was alarmed, because Gibeon was "a great city, like one of the royal cities", larger than Ai, with mighty men. He built a coalition of five kings, Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon, and aimed it at the defectors: "Come up and help me. We will attack Gibeon, because they have made peace with Joshua and the Israelites."

Gibeon's first act under the treaty was to collect on it. Their message to Gilgal was urgent: "Do not abandon your servants. Come quickly and save us! Help us, because all the kings of the Amorites from the hill country have joined forces against us." And Joshua, bound by an oath his men had sworn without asking God, marched all night from Gilgal with the whole army to defend the people who had tricked him. God's word for the night march came before the battle: "Do not be afraid of them, for I have delivered them into your hand. Not one of them shall stand against you."

Joshua caught the five armies by surprise after the all-night climb, and the LORD threw them into confusion. Israel routed them at Gibeon and pursued them up the ascent to Beth-horon and down the other side as far as Azekah and Makkedah. On the descent the battle left Israel's hands entirely: "As they fled before Israel along the descent from Beth-horon to Azekah, the LORD cast down on them large hailstones from the sky, and more of them were killed by the hailstones than by the swords of the Israelites."

Then Joshua prayed the most public prayer in the book, standing before Israel in the middle of a battle that needed more daylight than the day had: "O sun, stand still over Gibeon, O moon, over the Valley of Aijalon." The text answers with the event and its source in the same breath: "So the sun stood still and the moon stopped until the nation took vengeance upon its enemies. Is this not written in the Book of Jashar?" The narrator is quoting an older book of song, and the seam is left where any reader can see it. What the quotation says is this: "So the sun stopped in the middle of the sky and delayed going down about a full day." And the narrator's own verdict on the day outranks the astronomy: "There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD listened to the voice of a man, because the LORD fought for Israel."

The five kings, meanwhile, had run from the field and hidden in a cave at Makkedah. Joshua treated the cave as a holding cell, not a distraction: "Roll large stones against the mouth of the cave, and post men there to guard them." Then back to the pursuit: "Do not let them reach their cities, for the LORD your God has delivered them into your hand." Only when the slaughter was finished and the army had returned safely did he have the cave opened and the kings brought out. He called his commanders forward and made the victory physical and transferable: "Come here and put your feet on the necks of these kings." Then he handed them the charge he had lived under since the plains of Moab, now as something they could carry into every remaining battle: "Do not be afraid or discouraged". "Be strong and courageous, for the LORD will do this to all the enemies you fight."

The kings were killed and hung on five trees until evening, then taken down at sunset, as the law required, and thrown into the cave they had hidden in, and great stones were rolled against its mouth, and the narrator's refrain sounds: "the stones are there to this day."

What followed was a campaign at the speed of the narration itself, city after city in a wave. Makkedah fell that same day, its king treated as Jericho's had been. Libnah fell, no survivors. Lachish fell on the second day of its siege, and Horam king of Gezer, who came to help it, fell with his people. Eglon fell the day it was attacked. Hebron fell, its king and villages with it. Debir fell, the last name in the roll. The narrator keeps a single refrain running under the names, left no survivors, devoted to destruction, as he had done at the last city, and then gathers the whole sweep into one summary: "So Joshua conquered the whole region", the hill country, the Negev, the foothills, and the slopes, "together with all their kings", "leaving no survivors. He devoted to destruction everything that breathed, just as the LORD, the God of Israel, had commanded."

The geography runs from Kadesh-barnea to Gaza, and the whole region of Goshen as far as Gibeon, the city whose moldy bread had started this whole southern war. And the explanation the book gives for the speed is not Joshua's generalship: "And because the LORD, the God of Israel, fought for Israel, Joshua captured all these kings and their land in one campaign." Then Joshua returned with all Israel to the camp at Gilgal.

The south had fallen in a single campaign that began with a deception and a night march. But the kings of the north had been watching, and they were gathering a force the text will measure against the sand of the seashore.

title: The North Taken, and the List of Kings
subtitle: Joshua 11 to 12
description: Chariots at the waters of Merom, Hazor burned, a long war honestly recorded, and thirty-one kings counted like stones.
paragraphs: The south had fallen fast. The north would not. When Jabin king of Hazor heard what had happened, he built the largest coalition in the book: Jobab king of Madon, the kings of Shimron and Achshaph, the kings of the northern mountains and the Arabah and the foothills and Naphoth-dor, Canaanites east and west, Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites in the hill country, and Hivites at the foot of Hermon. Hazor was "formerly the head of all these kingdoms", and its king could summon a continent. What came out to meet Israel at the waters of Merom was "a multitude as numerous as the sand on the seashore, along with a great number of horses and chariots." The chariots matter. Israel had crossed the Jordan on foot; the north had the war technology of the age, and it had more of it than anyone could count.

God's word to Joshua the night before the battle carried a deadline and a strange order: "Do not be afraid of them, for by this time tomorrow I will deliver all of them slain before Israel. You are to hamstring their horses and burn up their chariots." Hamstring and burn. Israel was not to capture the north's military machine and keep it. The weapons that could have made Israel a power like its neighbors were to be destroyed on the field, by command.

Joshua attacked suddenly at Merom, and the coalition broke. The pursuit ran west "all the way to Greater Sidon and Misrephoth-maim, and eastward as far as the Valley of Mizpeh", and the text closes the battle the way it has closed them all: "They struck them down, leaving no survivors." Then Joshua did the strange order exactly: "Joshua treated them as the LORD had told him; he hamstrung their horses and burned up their chariots."

He turned back and took Hazor itself, put its king to the sword, and devoted everyone in it to destruction. "Nothing that breathed remained, and Joshua burned down Hazor itself." Of all the cities built on their mounds, Hazor alone was burned; the rest Israel occupied and plundered. The narrator pauses the campaign to certify the whole chain of command, and the sentence is the book's own audit of its hero: "As the LORD had commanded His servant Moses, so Moses commanded Joshua. That is what Joshua did, leaving nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses."

The summary that follows is careful with the map and with the calendar. The region taken ran from Mount Halak toward Seir in the south to Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon under Mount Hermon in the north, the hill country, the Negev, Goshen, the foothills, the Arabah, the mountains. And then, in one plain line that corrects any impression the southern blitz left: "Joshua waged war against all these kings for a long period of time." One campaign in the south. A long war in the north. The book keeps both tempos on the record.

It also records why no other city did what Gibeon had done: "No city made peace with the Israelites except the Hivites living in Gibeon; all others were taken in battle." And it gives the reason in its own theological voice, without flinching from it: "For it was of the LORD to harden their hearts to engage Israel in battle, so that they would be set apart for destruction and would receive no mercy, being annihilated as the LORD had commanded Moses." The Gibeonites feared and came with moldy bread. The rest hardened and came with chariots. The book sees God's hand in the difference, and says so.

One more enemy falls in this chapter, and they are the oldest fear in the story. The Anakim, the giants whose size melted the spies' hearts two generations earlier, were eliminated from the hill country of Hebron, Debir, and Anab, and from all the hill country of Judah and Israel. "No Anakim were left in the land of the Israelites; only in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod did any survive", three Philistine cities on the coast, where a remnant of the giants kept a foothold the book leaves for later generations to meet.

Then comes the sentence the whole first half of Joshua has been driving toward: "So Joshua took the entire land, in keeping with all that the LORD had spoken to Moses. And Joshua gave it as an inheritance to Israel according to the allotments to their tribes. Then the land had rest from war."

Chapter 12 is the monument to that rest, and it is built like the piles of stones at Gilgal: a list meant to be read as evidence. It begins east of the Jordan, with Moses' two kings. Sihon of Heshbon, whose territory ran from Aroer on the Arnon up to the Jabbok, half of Gilead, the Arabah down to the Salt Sea below Pisgah. And Og of Bashan, "one of the remnant of the Rephaim," ruling Hermon and Salecah and all Bashan to the borders of the Geshurites. Their land was already given away, to Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh.

Then the roll of the west, thirty-one names, each with its single word: the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, one; the king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one; Jarmuth, one; Lachish, one; Eglon, one; Gezer, one; Debir, one; Geder, one; Hormah, one; Arad, one; Libnah, one; Adullam, one; Makkedah, one; Bethel, one; Tappuah, one; Hepher, one; Aphek, one; Lasharon, one; Madon, one; Hazor, one; Shimron-meron, one; Achshaph, one; Taanach, one; Megiddo, one; Kedesh, one; Jokneam in Carmel, one; the king of Dor, one; the king of Goiim in Gilgal, one; and Tirzah, one. The list ends with its own count: "So there were thirty-one kings in all."

Read the roll slowly and it is a map and a memorial at once, city by city, the whole west bank measured in fallen thrones. But rest from war is not the same as a finished inheritance. The kings were dead; most of the land had not yet been divided, occupied, or even entered. And the next voice in the book is God's, speaking to an old man about everything that remains.

title: The Land Divided, and Caleb's Mountain
subtitle: Joshua 13 to 15
description: An old general, an older promise, an eighty-five-year-old asking for the giants' hill country, and Judah's hundred towns.
paragraphs: The second half of Joshua opens with age and unfinished business in the same sentence. Joshua was old and well along in years, and the LORD said to him: "You are old and well along in years, but very much of the land remains to be possessed." Then God Himself recites the remainder: all the territory of the Philistines and the Geshurites, from the Shihor east of Egypt to Ekron in the north, the five Philistine rulers of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron, the Avvites, the Canaanite coast up to Aphek, the Gebalites, and all Lebanon eastward to Lebo-hamath, and every Sidonian in the hill country. Over that unconquered map God laid a promise and a procedure: "All the inhabitants of the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim", He said, "all the Sidonians", "I Myself will drive out before the Israelites. Be sure to divide it by lot as an inheritance to Israel, as I have commanded you." Divide land you do not yet hold, to nine tribes and the half-tribe of Manasseh. The allotment was an act of war by other means, a deed drawn up in advance of the battles.

Before the new lots, the book re-surveys the old ones. East of the Jordan, Moses had already given the inheritance: Reuben on the plateau from Aroer on the Arnon through Heshbon's cities to the Jordan bank, Gad in Gilead and the valley towns up to the Sea of Chinnereth, the half-tribe of Manasseh through all of Bashan with its sixty cities of Jair. Two honest marks sit inside the survey. One is a name in the casualty list: "The Israelites also killed the diviner Balaam son of Beor along with the others they put to the sword", the prophet of Numbers who blessed Israel four times and died in Midian's camp anyway. The other is a failure that never got fixed: "but the Israelites did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites. So Geshur and Maacath dwell among the Israelites to this day." And twice, once for Moses' grants and once for the whole system, the survey repeats the exception at its center: "To the tribe of Levi, however, Moses had given no inheritance. The LORD, the God of Israel, is their inheritance, just as He had promised them."

The dividing west of the Jordan was done by Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the heads of the tribes, by lot, exactly as commanded. Joseph's line had become two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim, keeping the count at twelve inheritances with Levi landless. And before the first lot was cast, an old man walked up to Joshua at Gilgal with a claim older than the conquest.

Caleb son of Jephunneh had waited forty-five years to make this speech, and the text gives it to him nearly whole. "You know what the LORD said to Moses the man of God at Kadesh-barnea about you and me. I was forty years old when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land, and I brought back to him an honest report. Although my brothers who went with me made the hearts of the people melt with fear, I remained loyal to the LORD my God." The melting word again, the word that had traveled from the spies to Jericho to Ai, and Caleb names it as the thing he had refused to do. Then the oath: "On that day Moses swore to me, saying, 'Surely the land on which you have set foot will be an inheritance to you and your children forever, because you have wholly followed the LORD my God.'"

"Now behold, as the LORD promised, He has kept me alive these forty-five years since He spoke this word to Moses, while Israel wandered in the wilderness. So here I am today, eighty-five years old, still as strong today as I was the day Moses sent me out. As my strength was then, so it is now for war, for going out, and for coming in."

Then the ask, and it is not for rest or for a quiet valley: "Now therefore give me this hill country that the LORD promised me on that day, for you yourself heard then that the Anakim were there, with great and fortified cities. Perhaps with the LORD's help I will drive them out, as the LORD has spoken." The giants whose report had killed a generation were Caleb's chosen inheritance. Joshua blessed him and gave him Hebron, and the narrator writes the verdict the whole book has been building toward for this one man: "Hebron belongs to Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite as an inheritance to this day, because he wholly followed the LORD, the God of Israel." The chapter ends with the refrain: "Then the land had rest from war."

Judah's lot came first and largest, borders drawn from the southern tip of the Salt Sea along Edom's edge to the Brook of Egypt, up the Jordan mouth past the Valley of Achor and Gilgal, along the southern slope of Jebusite Jerusalem, and west to the Great Sea. Inside that allotment Caleb collected his promise personally. He drove the three sons of Anak out of Hebron, Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak himself, and then marched on Debir and offered his daughter Achsah in marriage to the man who took it. His nephew Othniel took it. Achsah then rode to her father with a request of her own, dismounted, and asked straight: "Give me a blessing". "Since you have given me land in the Negev, give me springs of water as well." Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs. In a book of borders, she is the one person who negotiates better land terms and gets them.

Judah's towns were counted by district, twenty-nine in the Negev, then the foothills in runs of fourteen, sixteen, and nine, Ekron and Ashdod and Gaza on the coast, the hill country in runs of eleven, nine, ten, six, and two, and six in the wilderness down to En-gedi, more than a hundred cities and villages in all. But the allotment's last line is the honest one, and it hangs over everything the lots will draw in the next chapters: "But the descendants of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem. So to this day the Jebusites live there among the descendants of Judah." The greatest tribe held the deed to Jerusalem, and foreigners still lived in it. The dividing of the land and the possessing of it were going to be two different stories.

title: Lots at Shiloh and the Cities of Refuge
subtitle: Joshua 16 to 21
description: Five sisters collect on a ruling, Joseph's sons are told to clear their own forest, forty-eight Levitical towns, and a verdict: not one promise failed.
paragraphs: After Judah, the lots turned to Joseph's house, the double tribe. Ephraim took the central hills from the Jordan at Jericho up through Bethel and down to Gezer and the sea, with cities of its own sprinkled inside Manasseh's borders. Manasseh took the long northern stretch from the sea up past Shechem and the Jordan, with assigned cities reaching into Issachar and Asher: Beth-shean, Ibleam, Dor, Endor, Taanach, Megiddo. And inside these two strong allotments the honest refrain of this whole section starts sounding. At Gezer, Ephraim's border city: "But they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer. So the Canaanites dwell among the Ephraimites to this day, but they are forced laborers." At Manasseh's northern cities the record is plainer still: the tribe "were unable to occupy these cities, because the Canaanites were determined to stay in this land", and when Israel grew stronger it settled for forced labor, "but they failed to drive them out completely."

Into the middle of Manasseh's allotment walk five women with a court ruling in their favor from a generation earlier. Zelophehad's daughters, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah, approached Eleazar, Joshua, and the leaders with a claim that quoted God's own decision: "The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brothers." They received it, shares among their father's brothers, and Manasseh's portion rose to ten shares because of them. The case those sisters had won before Moses in the wilderness was still paying out in land west of the Jordan.

Joseph's sons also brought Joshua a complaint, and his answer to it is the Caleb scene played backward. "Why have you given us only one portion as an inheritance? We have many people, because the LORD has blessed us abundantly." Joshua told them to take the forested hill country and clear it. They objected that the hill country was not enough and the valley was dangerous: "all the Canaanites who live in the valley have iron chariots, both in Beth-shean with its towns and in the Valley of Jezreel." Caleb, at eighty-five, had asked for the giants' hill country by name. The house of Joseph, numerous and strong, asked for a second portion that did not require fighting chariots. Joshua's final word gave them more land and no sympathy at all: "You have many people and great strength. You shall not have just one allotment, because the hill country will be yours as well. It is a forest; clear it, and its farthest limits will be yours. Although the Canaanites have iron chariots and although they are strong, you can drive them out."

The dividing then moved to Shiloh and slowed down. The whole congregation assembled there and set up the Tent of Meeting, the traveling sanctuary now planted in the land, "and though the land was subdued before them, there were still seven tribes of Israel who had not yet received their inheritance." Joshua's patience with the pause ran out in public: "How long will you put off entering and possessing the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you?" His method replaced waiting with walking: three men from each of the seven tribes, twenty-one surveyors, were sent to travel the remaining land, map it city by city in a written document, and divide it into seven portions, Judah holding the south and Joseph the north. They came back to Shiloh with the map, and Joshua cast the lots there, "in the presence of the LORD."

Benjamin drew first of the seven, a narrow inheritance wedged between Judah and Joseph, Jericho and Bethel and Gibeon among its twenty-six cities, and Jebus, which is Jerusalem. Then the lots finished the map in a run: Simeon, whose inheritance lay inside Judah's oversized territory; Zebulun toward the northern valleys; Issachar below Mount Tabor; Asher along the northern coast; Naphtali in the far north hills; and Dan, whose allotment proved too tight to hold, so that the Danites later went up and took Leshem in the far north and renamed it Dan after their father. Last of everyone, the leader was given his own: "the Israelites gave Joshua son of Nun an inheritance among them, as the LORD had commanded. They gave him the city of Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim, as he requested. He rebuilt the city and settled in it." The man who had divided a country asked for one town, and the survey closed: "So they finished dividing up the land."

Two institutions were planted before the division stood complete, and both were about the kind of country this would be. The first was the cities of refuge, designated "so that anyone who kills another unintentionally or accidentally may flee there. These will be your refuge from the avenger of blood." The procedure was law, not sanctuary by sentiment: the fugitive stated his case at the city gate before the elders, was taken in and given a place to live, and could not be surrendered to the avenger "because that man killed his neighbor accidentally without prior malice." He stayed until he stood trial before the assembly and until the death of the high priest, and only then went home. Six cities were set apart: Kedesh in Galilee, Shechem in Ephraim's hills, and Hebron in Judah, west of the Jordan; Bezer, Ramoth in Gilead, and Golan in Bashan, east of it. And the provision was written for "all the Israelites and foreigners among them," the same accidental killer, the same gate, the same hearing.

The second institution gave the landless tribe its scattering. The Levites came to Shiloh asking for what Moses had promised them, cities to live in with pastureland for their animals, and Israel gave them towns out of every tribe's inheritance. Aaron's priestly line drew thirteen, including Hebron, now a city of refuge, though its surrounding fields stayed Caleb's, as the text is careful to note. The rest of Kohath drew ten, Gershon thirteen, Merari twelve. The count closes at forty-eight cities in all, "within the territory of the Israelites", the tribe with no territory sprinkled through everyone else's.

Then the narrator steps back and reads the whole allotment as a verdict, and these are the sentences the division was built to reach: "Thus the LORD gave Israel all the land He had sworn to give their fathers, and they took possession of it and settled in it. And the LORD gave them rest on every side, just as He had sworn to their fathers. None of their enemies could stand against them, for the LORD delivered all their enemies into their hand." And the last word: "Not one of all the LORD's good promises to the house of Israel had failed; everything was fulfilled."

The same chapters had just recorded Canaanites holding Gezer, Megiddo, Beth-shean, and Jerusalem. The verdict and the failures stand in the same book without apology, because they measure different things. The allotment was complete and every tribe held its deed; the possession would take generations and some of it would never be finished. What had not failed was a promise. The land was given. What Israel would do with the giving was the question the rest of the Bible would spend itself answering. And the first test of the divided nation's unity was already on its way home, eastward, across the Jordan, where the two and a half tribes were about to build something by the river that their brothers would see as treason.

title: The Altar by the Jordan
subtitle: Joshua 22
description: A homecoming, an imposing altar, a nation arming for civil war, and an embassy that chose questions before swords.
paragraphs: The division was finished, and one promise from the plains of Moab was still outstanding. Joshua summoned the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, the tribes whose men had crossed the Jordan armed and fought for land that was never going to be theirs, and he released them with an audit that reads like a decoration: "You have done all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, and you have obeyed my voice in all that I commanded you. All this time you have not deserted your brothers, up to this very day, but have kept the charge given you by the LORD your God."

Their brothers had rest now, as promised, and the eastern men could go home. But Joshua sent them with the charge that echoes Deuteronomy's summary of the whole law: "But be very careful to observe the commandment and the law that Moses the servant of the LORD gave you: to love the LORD your God, to walk in all His ways, to keep His commandments, to hold fast to Him, and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul." He blessed them, and he loaded them: "Return to your homes with your great wealth, with immense herds of livestock, with silver, gold, bronze, iron, and very many clothes. Divide with your brothers the spoil of your enemies." The men who had left their families east of the river years earlier went home rich, to wives and children and herds that had grown up without them, in exchange for a war fought for other tribes' inheritances.

At Geliloth, near the Jordan, still in the land of Canaan on the crossing side, they stopped, and there the three tribes "built an imposing altar there by the Jordan." Not a small cairn. An imposing altar, big enough to be seen, big enough to be reported.

The report that reached Shiloh was accurate about the stones and assumed everything about the purpose: the eastern tribes "have built an altar on the border of the land of Canaan, at Geliloth near the Jordan on the Israelite side." The response was immediate and total: "the whole congregation of Israel assembled at Shiloh to go to war against them." One altar, seen from a distance, had Israel ready to fight its first civil war before the conquest generation had even settled.

But Israel did one thing right before it marched. It sent an embassy first: Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest, Aaron's grandson, with ten chiefs, one family head from each tribe. Phinehas had a history the book of Numbers recorded: at Peor he had stopped a plague with a spear. He was not a man sent to negotiate a compromise. He was sent to deliver an accusation, and the accusation was thorough: "What is this breach of faith you have committed today against the God of Israel by turning away from the LORD and building for yourselves an altar, that you might rebel against the LORD this day? Was not the sin of Peor enough for us, from which we have not cleansed ourselves to this day? It even brought a plague upon the congregation of the LORD."

Then the embassy did something remarkable inside its own indictment. It offered the accused an escape that would cost the accusers land: "If indeed the land of your inheritance is unclean, then cross over to the land of the LORD's possession, where the LORD's tabernacle stands, and take possession of it among us. But do not rebel against the LORD or against us by building for yourselves an altar other than the altar of the LORD our God." If your side of the river is the problem, they said, we will share our side. And they closed with the valley of Achor: "Was not Achan son of Zerah unfaithful regarding what was set apart for destruction, bringing wrath upon the whole congregation of Israel? Yet it was not only Achan who perished because of his sin!"

The eastern tribes answered with the strongest oath formula in the book, doubled: "The LORD, the Mighty One, is God! The LORD, the Mighty One, is God! He knows, and may Israel also know. If this was in rebellion or breach of faith against the LORD, do not spare us today." If they had built the altar to offer sacrifices on it, they said, "may the LORD Himself hold us accountable."

Then they explained, and the explanation reversed the whole picture. The altar was not for offerings at all. It was built out of fear, and the fear was aimed a generation ahead: "we have done this for fear that in the future your descendants might say to ours," and here the feared sentence stands as they quoted it: "What have you to do with the LORD, the God of Israel? For the LORD has made the Jordan a border between us and you Reubenites and Gadites. You have no share in the LORD!" The river that Israel had crossed on dry ground could become, in their grandchildren's mouth, a border of belonging. So they had built a replica where both sides would see it: "let it be a witness between us and you and the generations to come, that we will worship the LORD in His presence with our burnt offerings, sacrifices, and peace offerings", offered at God's own altar across the river, not on this one. And if the feared day ever came, their descendants could point at the stones and answer: "Look at the replica of the altar of the LORD that our fathers made, not for burnt offerings or sacrifices, but as a witness between us and you." They ended where the embassy had begun, with loyalty: "Far be it from us to rebel against the LORD and turn away from Him today by building an altar for burnt offerings, grain offerings, or sacrifices, other than the altar of the LORD our God, which stands before His tabernacle."

Phinehas heard it, and the priest who had once executed judgment at Peor now pronounced the all-clear: "Today we know that the LORD is among us, because you have not committed this breach of faith against Him. Consequently, you have delivered the Israelites from the hand of the LORD." The embassy rode home, the congregation heard the report and was satisfied, "they blessed God and spoke no more about going to war against them". The altar got its name from its builders: Witness. "It is a witness between us that the LORD is God."

One more pile of stones stood in Israel, then, and this one was a sermon rather than a memorial: a river is a boundary on a map, but it is not a border in the faith. The united nation had nearly gone to war over a misunderstanding, and what saved it was an embassy willing to accuse to the face, an offer willing to share land, and an explanation willing to be heard. It was the last act of the whole congregation together in the book, and it ended with a blessing instead of a battle.

title: Choose This Day
subtitle: Joshua 23 to 24
description: Two farewell speeches, God's own voice retelling the whole story, a vow priced before it was accepted, and three burials at Shechem.
paragraphs: A long time passed. The land rested, the surveyors' map became addresses, and Joshua grew old in the country he had divided. Then he called Israel together one more time, its elders, leaders, judges, and officers, and the speech he gave them was a farewell in the shape of Moses' own, because Joshua had been standing nearby when Moses gave his.

He began with their eyes: "you have seen everything that the LORD your God has done to all these nations for your sake, because it was the LORD your God who fought for you." The remaining nations were already allotted on paper, and God would drive them out as promised. What remained for Israel was the charge Joshua had received first for himself: "Be very strong, then, so that you can keep and obey all that is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, not turning aside from it to the right or to the left." No association with the nations left among them, no calling on their gods' names, no serving or bowing: "Instead, you shall hold fast to the LORD your God, as you have done to this day."

He reminded them of the arithmetic of the conquest: "One of you can put a thousand to flight, because the LORD your God fights for you, just as He promised." And he set the whole duty inside a single tender sentence: "Therefore watch yourselves carefully, that you love the LORD your God."

Then the warning, as plain as Deuteronomy's curses and aimed at assimilation rather than invasion: if you turn away and cling to the nations that remain, if you intermarry and associate with them, "know for sure that the LORD your God will no longer drive out these nations before you. Instead, they will become for you a snare and a trap, a scourge in your sides and thorns in your eyes, until you perish from this good land that the LORD your God has given you."

Joshua named his own death without ceremony: "Now behold, today I am going the way of all the earth, and you know with all your heart and soul that not one of the good promises the LORD your God made to you has failed. Everything was fulfilled for you; not one promise has failed." And then he turned the verdict over, the way a coin has two faces: "But just as every good thing the LORD your God promised you has come to pass, likewise the LORD will bring upon you the calamity He has threatened, until He has destroyed you from this good land He has given you."

The last assembly met at Shechem, the valley where Abraham had built his first altar in the land and where Jacob had buried foreign gods under an oak. All the tribes presented themselves before God, and Joshua let God tell the story. It runs in the first person, I took, I gave, I sent, I brought, across the whole history the reader of this book now carries: "Long ago your fathers, including Terah the father of Abraham and Nahor, lived beyond the Euphrates and worshiped other gods. But I took your father Abraham from beyond the Euphrates and led him through all the land of Canaan, and I multiplied his descendants." Isaac, then Jacob and Esau, Seir given to one and Egypt swallowing the others. "Then I sent Moses and Aaron, and I afflicted the Egyptians by what I did there, and afterward I brought you out." The sea brought over the pursuers. The wilderness years, the Amorite kings, Balak hiring a curse and getting blessings instead: "but I would not listen to Balaam. So he blessed you again and again, and I delivered you from his hand." The Jordan crossed, Jericho and the seven nations delivered, the hornet sent ahead: "I sent the hornet ahead of you, and it drove out the two Amorite kings before you, but not by your own sword or bow." And the summary of the gift, the line the entire recital was building toward: "So I gave you a land on which you did not toil and cities that you did not build, and now you live in them and eat from vineyards and olive groves that you did not plant."

Then Joshua turned God's history into Israel's decision: "Now, therefore, fear the LORD and serve Him in sincerity and truth; cast aside the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt, and serve the LORD." And he forced the choice into the open with the most famous sentence he ever spoke: "But if it is unpleasing in your sight to serve the LORD, then choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you are living. As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD!"

The people answered like the congregation at the Jordan's stones had taught them to answer: "Far be it from us to forsake the LORD to serve other gods!" They rehearsed their reasons, Egypt, the signs, the protection on the journey, the nations driven out, and landed it: "We too will serve the LORD, because He is our God!"

Joshua's response startles everyone who expects a leader to accept a pledge and close the meeting. He argued with their vow: "You are not able to serve the LORD, for He is a holy God; He is a jealous God; He will not forgive your rebellion or your sins. If you forsake the LORD and serve foreign gods, He will turn and bring disaster on you and consume you, even after He has been good to you." He was not discouraging them. He was pricing the promise, making sure the yes they were about to give was weighed, not warm. They gave it anyway, louder: "No!" "We will serve the LORD!"

Then Joshua told them: "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen to serve the LORD." "We are witnesses!" they said. He gave them the first act of the covenant, get rid of the foreign gods among you and incline your hearts to the LORD, and they answered with the final form of the pledge: "We will serve the LORD our God and obey His voice."

So Joshua made a covenant for the people that day at Shechem, set down a statute and ordinance, and recorded everything in the Book of the Law of God. And then, one last time in this book, somebody set up a stone. Joshua took a large stone and raised it under the oak near the sanctuary of the LORD, and he told the assembly what it was for: "You see this stone. It will be a witness against us, for it has heard all the words the LORD has spoken to us, and it will be a witness against you if you ever deny your God." Twelve stones at Gilgal, a pile in Achor, a pile at Ai's gate, a cave sealed at Makkedah, an altar named Witness by the Jordan, and now a stone under the oak at Shechem. Joshua's whole leadership can be read in rock: each one a place where God had acted and Israel had answered, set up so that forgetting would have to walk past evidence.

Then he sent the people away, each to his own inheritance, and the book closes with three burials. "Some time later, Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of 110." He was buried at Timnath-serah, the town he had asked for, in the hill country of Ephraim. The assistant who had stood at Moses' elbow carried Moses' own title at the end, servant of the LORD, and the narrator's judgment on his era is one calm line: "Israel had served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him and who had experienced all the works that the LORD had done for Israel."

The second burial reached back furthest. "And the bones of Joseph, which the Israelites had brought up out of Egypt, were buried at Shechem in the plot of land that Jacob had purchased from the sons of Hamor," the field at the same Shechem where Israel had just renewed the covenant. Joseph had made his brothers swear to carry his bones up when God came to them, back in the last chapter of Genesis, and the promise had traveled through slavery, exodus, wilderness, and conquest, and it came to rest in the ground a few steps from the witness stone. The third burial was Eleazar son of Aaron, laid in the hill country at Gibeah, the town given to his son Phinehas, the priest who had carried the embassy to the altar by the Jordan.

The book ends with the land divided, the covenant renewed, the witnesses in place, and the generation that had seen the Jordan stop now under the ground it had inherited. Everything depended on whether the children who would ask about the stones would give the answer their fathers rehearsed. The next book opens with the words this one has been holding back since its first line, and they are almost the same words: after the death of Joshua.
